entries.sentence: The NHS says the symptoms of osteoarthritis may come and go in episodes.
entries.note: NHS symptoms page: symptoms may come and go in episodes.

entries.sentence: These episodes can be linked to how active a person has been, and even to the weather.
entries.note: NHS symptoms page: related to activity levels and even the weather.

entries.sentence: Pain and stiffness are the main features.
entries.note: Summary: pain and stiffness are the main features.

entries.sentence: Joints near the ends of the fingers, the base of the thumb, the neck, the lower back, the knees and the hips are the ones most often affected.
entries.note: NHS symptoms page lists these joints.

entries.sentence: One UK source describes bad spells lasting weeks or months, broken up by better periods.
entries.note: Search 'summary' blended pages and did not name the page for this point; returned excerpt attributed to a UK source; attribution to NHS inform is likely but not certain.

entries.sentence: The NHS says the condition does not necessarily get worse over time.
entries.note: Summary of NHS treatment page: condition does not necessarily get any worse over time.

entries.sentence: Another source says movement may become limited over time, but that treatment usually improves how well the joint works.
entries.note: Search 'summary' blended pages and did not name the page for this point; summary said another source says movement may become limited but treatment usually improves function.

entries.sentence: How bad the symptoms are does not always match what a scan shows.
entries.note: Search 'summary' blended pages and did not name the page for this point; summary: severity does not track imaging.

entries.sentence: Some people have clear changes on an X-ray but only mild symptoms, while others have severe symptoms with little change to see.
entries.note: Search 'summary' blended pages and did not name the page for this point; summary: significant X-ray changes with mild symptoms and vice versa.

entries.sentence: A GP can often diagnose osteoarthritis from what a person says about their symptoms, their medical history and what the GP sees when examining the joints.
entries.note: Summary: GP likely to diagnose based on symptoms, history and examination; blended pages.

entries.sentence: There is no single test that confirms it.
entries.note: Search 'summary' blended pages and did not name the page for this point; summary: no single definitive test.

entries.sentence: Imaging is only occasionally used, either to support the diagnosis or to rule out other problems.
entries.note: Summary: imaging occasionally used to support or rule out other problems.

entries.sentence: Blood tests do not diagnose osteoarthritis, but they can look for other conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or gout.
entries.note: Search 'summary' blended pages and did not name the page for this point; summary: blood tests don't diagnose but look for alternatives such as rheumatoid arthritis or gout.

entries.sentence: X-rays are often not needed to diagnose the condition.
entries.note: Summary quotes: X-rays are often not needed to diagnose osteoarthritis.

entries.sentence: A doctor may suggest an X-ray or other tests when unsure of the diagnosis and wanting to rule out other problems.
entries.note: Summary quote: sometimes your doctor may suggest X-rays or other tests if uncertain.

entries.sentence: Scans also often show changes in people who have no symptoms at all.
entries.note: Search 'summary' blended pages and did not name the page for this point; summary: scans often show changes in people with no symptoms.

entries.sentence: The NHS advises seeing a GP when symptoms of osteoarthritis persist, so the diagnosis can be confirmed and any needed treatment arranged.
entries.note: Summary: NHS advises seeing GP if persistent symptoms to confirm diagnosis and prescribe treatment; page not named.

entries.sentence: The NHS describes three strands of treatment: lifestyle measures, medicines to relieve pain, and supportive therapies.
entries.note: NHS treatment page via summary.

entries.sentence: Exercise is described as a core treatment, alongside ways to reduce stress on the joints.
entries.note: Summary: exercise is a core treatment alongside efforts to decrease joint stress.

entries.sentence: For pain in the knees and hands, creams containing an anti-inflammatory medicine (topical NSAIDs) are generally favoured.
entries.note: Summary: topical NSAIDs generally favoured for knees and hands.

entries.sentence: An NHS England document says they have fewer side effects than NSAID tablets.
entries.note: Summary: NHS England document says fewer side effects and safer than NSAID tablets.

entries.sentence: Capsaicin cream may also help, and a burning feeling when it is applied is common.
entries.note: Summary: capsaicin cream can help; burning sensation common.

entries.sentence: The NHS suggests paracetamol for short-term pain but notes that many people find it does not work very well.
entries.note: Summary: NHS guidance suggests it for short-term pain but many find it doesn't work well.

entries.sentence: If creams and paracetamol are not enough, a GP may prescribe anti-inflammatory tablets, usually with a second medicine to protect the stomach.
entries.note: Summary: oral NSAIDs usually with a proton pump inhibitor.

entries.sentence: Stronger painkillers such as codeine are used for severe pain, generally for short periods because of side effects.
entries.note: Summary: opioids such as codeine for severe pain, generally short-term.

entries.sentence: Steroid injections go directly into the joint and are usually offered when other treatments have not worked.
entries.note: Summary: steroid injections into the joint, usually when others haven't worked.

entries.sentence: The NHS says they can reduce pain for up to three months.
entries.note: Summary: can reduce pain for up to 3 months.

entries.sentence: The NHS describes self-help measures such as pacing activities, using a walking stick and wearing suitable footwear to reduce stress on an affected joint.
entries.note: Summary: reducing stress on the joint, pacing, walking stick, suitable footwear.

entries.sentence: Physiotherapists can also advise on supports and braces.
entries.note: Summary: physiotherapists can advise on supports and braces.

entries.sentence: Other sources mention heat or cold packs for pain, shoe inserts or braces for standing and walking, and self-management classes.
entries.note: Search 'summary' blended pages and did not name the page for this point; summary lists hot/cold packs, assistive devices, inserts, braces, classes across sources.

entries.sentence: One source notes that the pain can wake a person at night even when the joint is resting.
entries.note: Search 'summary' blended pages and did not name the page for this point; summary: pain can wake you at night even when the joint is rested.

entries.sentence: GPs no longer prescribe glucosamine and chondroitin supplements on the NHS, because there is no strong evidence they work.
entries.note: Summary: GPs no longer prescribe chondroitin and glucosamine on the NHS; no strong evidence.

entries.sentence: An NHS England decision aid says hyaluronic acid injections do not help knee osteoarthritis.
entries.note: Summary of NHS England decision aid.

entries.sentence: It also says there is no good evidence for TENS machines, acupuncture or insoles, although another NHS source lists TENS as a physiotherapy option.
entries.note: Summary: NHS England says no good evidence; another NHS source lists TENS.

entries.sentence: The NHS says surgery is kept for a small number of cases where other treatments have not helped or daily life is seriously affected.
entries.note: Summary: reserved for small number of cases.

entries.sentence: Most people with osteoarthritis do not need surgery.
entries.note: Summary: most people do not need surgery.

entries.sentence: Referral is to an orthopaedic surgeon, a doctor who specialises in bone and joint operations.
entries.note: Summary: referral to an orthopaedic surgeon; definition of the term is general knowledge (textbook).

entries.sentence: The options include fusion of a joint and joint replacement.
entries.note: Summary: options include osteotomy, fusion and joint replacement; osteotomy left out because the text gave no definition.

entries.sentence: An NHS commissioning document says many people avoid joint surgery by combining pain relief, lifestyle changes, weight reduction and exercise.
entries.note: Summary: NHS-style document (North Yorkshire CCG knee replacement leaflet); says many people avoid surgery with pain relief, lifestyle changes, weight reduction and exercise.

entries.sentence: The same document quotes a conclusion that weight loss and exercise together gave similar symptom relief to joint replacement.
entries.note: Summary: weight loss plus exercise achieved same symptom relief as replacement per quoted conclusion in one NHS document.

entries.sentence: It lists blood clots in the leg veins (deep vein thrombosis) and wound problems among the early complications of joint replacement.
entries.note: Summary: NHS document lists DVT and wound complications as common early complications; DVT definition paraphrased from summary wording only.

entries.sentence: The NHS says there is no cure for osteoarthritis, but its symptoms can be managed.
entries.note: Summary: no cure but symptoms can be managed.

entries.sentence: It also says the condition does not necessarily get worse over time.
entries.note: Summary of NHS treatment page.

entries.sentence: Treatment combines lifestyle measures, pain-relieving medicines and supportive therapies.
entries.note: NHS three strands.

entries.sentence: Exercise is described as a core treatment alongside ways to reduce stress on the joints.
entries.note: Summary: exercise is a core treatment.

entries.sentence: Sources say X-rays are often not needed, because the diagnosis can usually be made from the symptoms and an examination.
entries.note: Summary: X-rays often not needed; GP can diagnose from symptoms and exam.

entries.sentence: A doctor may suggest one if the diagnosis is uncertain or other problems need ruling out.
entries.note: Summary quote.

entries.sentence: One hand-focused source says an X-ray showing osteoarthritis does not mean a person will have problems.
entries.note: Search 'summary' blended pages and did not name the page for this point; summary attributed this to a hand source (likely an NHS hand page).

entries.sentence: Sources say severity does not always match imaging.
entries.note: Search 'summary' blended pages and did not name the page for this point; summary: severity doesn't track imaging.

entries.sentence: Some people have major changes on an X-ray with mild symptoms, and others have severe symptoms with little visible change.
entries.note: Search 'summary' blended pages and did not name the page for this point; summary.

entries.sentence: Imaging is only occasionally used, either to support the diagnosis or to rule out other problems.
entries.note: Summary: imaging occasionally used.

entries.note: Search 'summary' blended pages and did not name the page for this point; summary.

entries.sentence: The NHS says GPs no longer prescribe them, because there is no strong evidence that they work as a treatment for osteoarthritis.
entries.note: Summary: GPs no longer prescribe; no strong evidence.

entries.sentence: Treatment options the NHS does describe include exercise, creams, pain-relieving medicines and supportive therapies.
entries.note: Summary of NHS treatment page.

entries.sentence: An NHS England decision aid also says hyaluronic acid injections do not help knee osteoarthritis.
entries.note: Summary of NHS England decision aid.

entries.sentence: No. Sources say most people with osteoarthritis do not need surgery.
entries.note: Summary: most people do not need surgery.

entries.note: Summary.

entries.sentence: An orthopaedic surgeon would then discuss the options, which include joint replacement.
entries.note: Summary.

entries.note: Summary: North Yorkshire CCG NHS leaflet.

entries.note: NHS symptoms page lists these.

entries.note: NHS symptoms.

entries.note: Summary.

contradictions: Existing entry lists paracetamol as a pain option without caveat; NHS treatment page (via summary) says many people find it does not work very well, and an NHS England decision aid says there is no good evidence it helps and long-term use might be harmful.
Existing definition calls osteoarthritis 'progressive'; NHS says (via summary) it does not necessarily get any worse over time.
